title: 1796 — Jenner and the Cowpox Experiment
d: The first documented vaccination: Edward Jenner's test of cowpox against smallpox.
definition: The first documented vaccination: Edward Jenner's test of cowpox against smallpox.
description:
In May 1796, English physician Edward Jenner inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with matter from a cowpox sore on milkmaid Sarah Nelmes, then later exposed him to smallpox — the boy did not fall ill. Jenner published his findings in 1798. He did not know what a virus was; he knew only that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed spared by smallpox. The word 'vaccine' comes from 'vacca', Latin for cow. Within a few years, vaccination spread across Europe and to the Americas, and it became the template for everything immunology would later become.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Jenner combined country observation (milkmaids' immunity) with a deliberate human experiment, then published for others to replicate. The method — expose to a related mild agent to gain protection — preceded germ theory by 70 years.

APPLICATIONS. Vaccination as a practice; the template for every vaccine that followed; the eventual eradication of smallpox.
how_it_works: Jenner combined country observation (milkmaids' immunity) with a deliberate human experiment, then published for others to replicate. The method — expose to a related mild agent to gain protection — preceded germ theory by 70 years.
applications: Vaccination as a practice; the template for every vaccine that followed; the eventual eradication of smallpox.

title: 1892-1898 — The Discovery of Viruses (Ivanovsky and Beijerinck)
t: 1892-1898 — The Discovery of Viruses (Ivanovsky and Beijerinck)
d: How a sick tobacco plant revealed an entirely new kind of infectious agent.
definition: How a sick tobacco plant revealed an entirely new kind of infectious agent.
description:
In 1892, Russian botanist Dmitri Ivanovsky filtered sap from diseased tobacco plants through bacteria-proof filters — and the sap stayed infectious. In 1898, Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck repeated the work, showed the agent diffused like a fluid, and called it 'contagium vivum fluidum' — a contagious living fluid. He named the mosaic disease's cause a virus. Nothing this small had ever been conceived: an infectious agent far below bacteria, invisible to every microscope of the age. The tobacco mosaic virus became the founding member of virology.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Filtration experiments separated the agent from bacteria by size; diffusion tests showed it behaved unlike particles. Two independent researchers, six years apart, converged on the same impossible conclusion.

APPLICATIONS. The birth of virology; the concept of filterable agents; the start of a century of virus hunting.

applications: The birth of virology; the concept of filterable agents; the start of a century of virus hunting.

title: 1885 — Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine
d: The first laboratory-made vaccine given after exposure — and it worked.
definition: The first laboratory-made vaccine given after exposure — and it worked.
description:
In July 1885, 9-year-old Joseph Meister was mauled by a rabid dog. His mother brought him to Louis Pasteur, who had been attenuating rabies in rabbit spinal cords. Over ten days Pasteur gave the boy 13 injections of increasingly potent preparations. Meister lived. Pasteur had previously shown the method protected dogs. The success made Pasteur a world figure and founded the Pasteur Institute. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis — wound care plus vaccine — remains the documented life-saving response to this day.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Serial passage through rabbits attenuated the virus; graded dosing built immunity faster than the slow infection could kill. It was immunology by courage and arithmetic.

APPLICATIONS. Post-exposure prophylaxis; the Pasteur Institute; proof that vaccines could follow exposure, not just precede it.

title: 1898 — The First Animal Virus (Loeffler and Frosch)
t: 1898 — The First Animal Virus (Loeffler and Frosch)
d: Foot-and-mouth disease proved viruses infect animals too.
definition: Foot-and-mouth disease proved viruses infect animals too.
description:
Friedrich Loeffler and Paul Frosch, working in Germany, showed that foot-and-mouth disease — a devastating livestock plague — passed through bacteria-proof filters. It was the first documented animal virus, found the same year Beijerinck named plant viruses. The discovery mattered economically as much as scientifically: foot-and-mouth could ruin farming regions, and knowing the enemy was filterable changed veterinary science.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). The same filtration logic Ivanovsky used, applied to cattle disease. Veterinary virology was born alongside human virology.

APPLICATIONS. Veterinary virology; livestock disease control; the economic case for virus research.

title: 1900-1901 — The Reed Commission and Yellow Fever
t: 1900-1901 — The Reed Commission and Yellow Fever
d: The first human virus proven to spread by an insect.
definition: The first human virus proven to spread by an insect.
description:
Walter Reed's commission in Cuba tested Carlos Finlay's mosquito hypothesis with human volunteers — some sleeping in mosquito-proof rooms, others exposed to infected mosquitoes. The results were decisive: Aedes mosquitoes transmitted yellow fever. Volunteer Jesse Lazear died of the disease during the work. Screens, drainage and quarantine followed, and Havana's yellow fever faded. It was the first documented proof that an insect could carry a human virus.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Controlled human exposure experiments with screened vs. unscreened quarters — epidemiology as experimental science, at great personal cost.

APPLICATIONS. Vector-borne disease science; mosquito control; the model for proving transmission routes.

title: 1908 — Landsteiner Proves Polio Is Viral
d: Karl Landsteiner and Erwin Popper transmitted polio to monkeys.
definition: Karl Landsteiner and Erwin Popper transmitted polio to monkeys.
description:
By grinding the spinal cord of a polio victim, filtering it, and injecting it into monkeys, Karl Landsteiner and Erwin Popper produced the disease in 1908 — proving poliomyelitis was caused by a filterable virus. It was painstaking, unglamorous work that gave researchers an animal model and, decades later, the foundation for vaccines.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Filtration plus animal inoculation: the classic early-20th-century proof of a viral cause.

APPLICATIONS. Polio virology; the animal-model method; the long road to the Salk and Sabin vaccines.

title: 1911 — Rous Discovers a Tumor Virus
d: A chicken sarcoma that could be transmitted by cell-free filtrate.
definition: A chicken sarcoma that could be transmitted by cell-free filtrate.
description:
Peyton Rous showed that a sarcoma in chickens could be transmitted using filtrates containing no intact cells — the first documented tumor-causing virus, Rous sarcoma virus. The finding was so far ahead of its time that it took 55 years to earn him the Nobel Prize (1966). It founded the field of tumor virology and eventually led to the discovery of oncogenes.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Cell-free transmission of cancer — an idea the field resisted for half a century before molecular biology vindicated it.

title: 1917 — d'Herelle and the Bacteriophages
d: Viruses that eat bacteria — discovered in soldier's stool.
definition: Viruses that eat bacteria — discovered in soldier's stool.
description:
French-Canadian microbiologist Félix d'Hérelle, studying dysentery among soldiers, noticed clear spots in bacterial cultures — zones where something had killed the bacteria. He called them bacteriophages, 'bacteria eaters'. Frederick Twort had seen something similar in 1915. Phages turned out to be the most numerous biological entities on Earth, and they became the laboratory workhorses of molecular biology.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Plaque observation on bacterial lawns — the clear-zone method that became virology's counting tool.

title: 1935 — Stanley Crystallizes a Virus
d: Tobacco mosaic virus turned out to be a chemical you could crystallize.
definition: Tobacco mosaic virus turned out to be a chemical you could crystallize.
description:
Wendell Stanley purified tobacco mosaic virus and grew it into crystals — showing that a virus was largely protein and behaved like a chemical, not a fluid mystery. d: A vaccine so good one dose protects for decades.
definition: A vaccine so good one dose protects for decades.
description:

title: 1949 — Growing Polio in a Dish (Enders, Weller, Robbins)
t: 1949 — Growing Polio in a Dish (Enders, Weller, Robbins)
d: Tissue culture made modern vaccines possible.
definition: Tissue culture made modern vaccines possible.
description:
John Enders, Thomas Weller and Frederick Robbins showed poliovirus could be grown in human tissue culture — no monkeys required. The 1954 Nobel Prize followed. title: 1952 — Hershey and Chase: DNA Is the Genetic Material
t: 1952 — Hershey and Chase: DNA Is the Genetic Material
d: A blender experiment with phages settled biology's biggest question.
definition: A blender experiment with phages settled biology's biggest question.
description:
Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase infected bacteria with bacteriophages whose protein was radioactively labeled in one batch and whose DNA was labeled in another, then used a kitchen blender to shear the phage coats off. Only the DNA entered the cells. DNA — not protein — carried heredity. The phage, a virus, answered the question for all of life.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Differential radioactive labeling plus mechanical shearing — elegant, cheap, decisive.

APPLICATIONS. Molecular biology's founding experiment; DNA's confirmation as the molecule of heredity.

title: 1952 — Dulbecco's Plaque Assay
d: Counting viruses the way you count colonies.
definition: Counting viruses the way you count colonies.

APPLICATIONS. Quantitative virology; vaccine potency testing; every titer measurement since.

title: 1955 and 1961 — Salk and Sabin Defeat Polio's Terror
t: 1955 and 1961 — Salk and Sabin Defeat Polio's Terror
d: Two vaccines, two philosophies, one collapsing disease.
definition: Two vaccines, two philosophies, one collapsing disease.
description:
Jonas Salk's killed-virus injectable vaccine was declared safe and effective in 1955 after the largest field trial in history (1.8 million children). Albert Sabin's live oral vaccine followed in 1961 — easier to give, better at blocking transmission. Together they drove polio down ~99% worldwide. The rivalry between the two men was as famous as the science.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Killed vs. live-attenuated: Salk's safety-first injection, Sabin's transmission-blocking drink.

APPLICATIONS. Near-eradication of polio; the largest clinical trial ever run; the vaccine-rivalry legend.

title: 1964 — Epstein-Barr: The First Human Tumor Virus
t: 1964 — Epstein-Barr: The First Human Tumor Virus

definition: A virus from African children's tumors.
description:
Denis Burkitt noticed clusters of jaw tumors in African children and suspected an infectious cause. Michael Epstein, Yvonne Barr and Bert Achong found herpesvirus particles in the tumor cells — Epstein-Barr virus, the first virus documented to cause human cancer. t: 1965-1981 — Blumberg, Hepatitis B, and the First Anti-Cancer Vaccine
d: A blood-bank curiosity became a cancer-preventing vaccine.
definition: A blood-bank curiosity became a cancer-preventing vaccine.

Baruch Blumberg found an odd antigen in an Australian aborigine's blood — the 'Australia antigen', later the hepatitis B surface protein (Nobel 1976). It enabled blood screening, then a vaccine: first plasma-derived (1981), then recombinant. Because chronic HBV causes liver cancer, the HBV vaccine was the first vaccine documented to prevent a human cancer.

definition: SARS, MERS, then the pandemic.
description:
SARS (2003) was contained by public health alone. MERS (2012) smoldered from camels. Then SARS-CoV-2 (identified January 2020) became the first coronavirus pandemic — and the fastest vaccine development ever documented, from genome publication (Jan 10, 2020) to authorization (December 2020). Coronaviruses went from obscure cold viruses to the most studied virus family on Earth.

HOW IT WORKS (as a concept). Rapid genome sharing (GISAID) plus platform vaccine technologies built on decades of coronavirus research.

APPLICATIONS. Pandemic preparedness; mRNA platforms; the value of studying 'obscure' viruses before they matter.
